title: Thermal Performance, Heat Flux Distribution, and Primary Energy Implications of Active Heated Triple-Glazed Units: Localized vs. Full-Surface Operation
content: This study conducts a comparative empirical evaluation of spatial heat flux distribution, cavity thermofluid dynamics, and primary energy implications in an argon-filled triple-glazed unit (TGU) operating under localized bottom-edge perimeter heating (configuration I) and full-surface planar heating (configuration II) across outdoor temperatures ranging from -25 °C to +5 °C. Empirical boundary-layer measurements from a physical test specimen (Asample= 0.405 m2) were scaled to a standard architectural reference module (A = 2.5 m2). To establish a dimensionally valid comparison against whole-building regulatory NZEB limits, module energy demands were normalized by gross conditioned floor area using a representative fenestration-to-conditioned-floor-area ratio of 0.2. Results demonstrate that localized perimeter heating acts as an exergy-efficient micro-climate buffer, achieving a 34% reduction in inward heat loss when increasing the foil setpoint from 30 °C to 45 °C and effectively suppressing cold downdraughts while restricting floor-area-normalized primary energy demand to 11.4 kWh/m2∙yr  (EPpoint = 143 kWh/yr total module demand across an 864 h duty cycle).  In contrast, full-surface heating eliminates vertical thermal stratification and achieves spatial temperature homogeneity, but converts the glazing into an active space heater, driving high internal heat flux densities (182.1–234.5 W/m² at -25 °C) and an annual primary energy consumption of 1188 kWh/yr per module (EPplanar = 95.04 kWh/m2∙yr, representing an 8.3-fold increase compared to configuration I (143 kWh/yr total module demand). This 8.3-fold discrepancy confirms that unmodulated full-surface planar heating acts as a high-penalty primary energy load, requiring model predictive control architectures to decouple peak thermal capacity from cumulative primary energy constraints. Exterior glass surface temperatures remain thermally independent of internal heating across both regimes, and argon cavity Rayleigh numbers from 2.5 x 104 to 5 x 104 confirm a stable convective boundary-layer regime. To comply with nearly zero-energy building (NZEB) standards, an intelligent model predictive control  strategy should maintain localized perimeter heating as a low-power baseline, dynamically escalating to full-surface heating only during extreme sub-zero climatic conditions.
